title: Transformer-Based Scientific Paper Recommendation via Contextual Neural Embeddings
abstract: We present a transformer-based recommendation system that retrieves and ranks scientific papers using contextual embeddings derived from SciBERT and fine-tuned with domain-specific contrastive objectives. The system encodes title and abstract into 768-dimensional vectors indexed with FAISS, with citation co-occurrence used as a weak supervision signal. Evaluated on five cross-domain benchmarks, it outperforms prior retrieval and recommendation baselines by 8–14% nDCG.

components.evidence: The system retrieves candidate papers from a large corpus using a bi-encoder architecture with FAISS approximate nearest-neighbour indexing; retrieval is the primary pipeline stage before re-ranking.
SciBERT is fine-tuned end-to-end with a contrastive InfoNCE loss over (query paper, relevant paper, hard negative) triples; the model architecture and training recipe are the core contribution.
Papers are represented as 768-dimensional dense embeddings of title and abstract; these embeddings are the retrieval artifact stored in the FAISS index.
The recommendation engine ranks candidate papers by cosine similarity to an embedding of the user's reading history, combining retrieval scores with a lightweight learning-to-rank layer.
Citation co-occurrence pairs serve as weak positive supervision during contrastive pre-training; the citation graph is not analysed structurally beyond this signal.

title: Graph Neural Networks for Citation Network Representation Learning
abstract: We propose a graph neural network architecture that learns node representations over academic citation graphs by aggregating both local neighbourhood structure and global bibliometric signals. The model is evaluated on node classification (field-of-study prediction) and link prediction (citation recommendation) tasks across four large citation corpora, achieving state-of-the-art results on all benchmarks.

components.evidence: Retrieval is not the primary concern; the paper frames citation recommendation as a link prediction task on a static graph rather than a retrieval problem over a document corpus.
Paper titles are encoded by a lightweight frozen text encoder to initialise node features; the NLM is an input pre-processing step rather than a core methodological contribution.
Node embeddings in the citation graph double as document representations and are evaluated on downstream classification tasks, providing a form of scientific document embedding via graph propagation.
The authors suggest learned embeddings could feed a recommendation pipeline but do not implement or evaluate a full recommendation system; the paper stops at representation learning.

The core contribution is a GNN that propagates information through directed citation edges and undirected co-authorship links, with analysis of degree distributions and structural properties across four citation corpora.

title: Dense Retrieval for Scientific Literature: A Contrastive Learning Approach
abstract: We develop a dense retrieval system for scientific corpora using domain-adapted dual encoders trained with contrastive objectives and hard-negative mining from BM25 candidates. The system is benchmarked on five scientific retrieval datasets and outperforms BM25, ColBERT, and DPR baselines. Ablations confirm the importance of domain-specific pre-training and hard-negative curriculum scheduling.

components.evidence: Dense retrieval over scientific corpora is the central and sole contribution; the entire paper is organised around improving retrieval precision and recall on scientific benchmarks.
The dual-encoder architecture uses SciBERT as the backbone; domain adaptation via continued pre-training on scientific text is a key ablation studied in the paper.
Documents are indexed as dense vectors in a FAISS index; producing high-quality scientific document embeddings through contrastive learning is the core technical objective.
Paper recommendation is one of five downstream evaluations; the retrieval model is applied to recommendation by treating a researcher's prior papers as the query.
Citation data is used only to sample hard negatives during contrastive training; no structural citation analysis is performed.

title: Federated Learning for Privacy-Preserving Clinical Text Classification
abstract: We present a federated learning framework that distributes NLP model training across hospital sites without centralising patient text. ClinicalBERT is fine-tuned under federated gradient aggregation with differential privacy guarantees, evaluated on ICD-10 coding and 30-day readmission prediction across six hospital datasets.

components.evidence: Document retrieval is not addressed; the paper is entirely focused on classification under privacy constraints rather than retrieval from a corpus.
ClinicalBERT is fine-tuned under federated gradient aggregation; NLMs are used as a tool for classification rather than being the subject of study.
No general-purpose document embeddings are produced; the model outputs task-specific logits for classification targets.
No recommendation component is present; the paper addresses classification tasks in a privacy-constrained federated setting.
Citation networks are absent from the methodology and evaluation; the paper operates entirely on clinical text corpora.

title: Collaborative Filtering with Semantic User Profiles for Research Discovery
abstract: We propose a hybrid recommendation method that combines collaborative filtering signals with semantic embeddings of user publication histories. User profiles are constructed from abstract embeddings of a researcher's prior papers; a collaborative filtering objective then surfaces relevant unseen papers. Evaluated on 50k researcher profiles, the method improves over pure collaborative filtering and pure content-based baselines.

components.evidence: A BM25 retrieval stage generates candidate papers before semantic re-ranking; retrieval is a pipeline component rather than the primary contribution.
User profile embeddings are computed from paper abstracts using a frozen language model; the NLM is used as a feature extractor rather than being trained end-to-end.
Paper embeddings are used for semantic re-ranking but are derived from a pre-trained general-purpose model without domain adaptation.
The core contribution is a collaborative filtering objective augmented with semantic user profile vectors, directly targeting research paper recommendation.
Citation data is not used; the model relies on co-reading signals and download logs as implicit feedback.

title: Multi-Modal Scientific Document Representation with Cross-Attention Fusion
abstract: We introduce a multi-modal representation model that fuses text, figures, and tables from scientific documents using cross-attention layers between a Longformer text encoder and a ViT image encoder. The unified dense embedding achieves state-of-the-art results on retrieval and classification benchmarks, outperforming text-only and late-fusion baselines.

components.evidence: The model is benchmarked primarily on retrieval tasks including SciFact and five BEIR-Science subsets; retrieval performance is the headline evaluation metric.
Longformer is used as the text encoder; cross-attention fusion between Longformer and ViT is the central architectural contribution.
The primary output is a single dense embedding of the full scientific document across text, figure, and table modalities, directly targeting multi-modal document representation.
The embeddings are evaluated on a paper recommendation task using a held-out academic dataset; recommendation is one of four downstream evaluations.
Citation relationships are used to construct train/test splits that prevent data leakage, but citation structure is not part of the model or its evaluation metrics.

title: Decentralized Research Data Repositories: Blockchain Provenance and Retrieval Primitives
abstract: We design a blockchain-based architecture for decentralized research data provenance tracking. Data artifacts are registered on a permissioned ledger with Merkle-tree integrity proofs; retrieval primitives allow auditors to locate and verify any version of a dataset by cryptographic hash. The system is evaluated on reproducibility workflows across three scientific domains.

components.evidence: Retrieval primitives are defined for locating data artifacts by cryptographic hash in a distributed ledger. These are infrastructure-level hash lookups rather than semantic search over document content — the paper uses the word 'retrieval' in a storage/provenance sense, not the IR sense.
No neural language models are employed; data access and integrity are governed entirely by smart contract logic and cryptographic proofs.
Documents are represented by cryptographic hashes for integrity verification; no dense embedding or semantic representation is produced.
No recommendation component is present; the paper addresses data provenance, access control, and reproducibility rather than discovery or ranking.
Citation chains are tracked as provenance edges in the blockchain DAG for reproducibility auditing; this is structural provenance tracking, not citation graph analysis for bibliometric insight.

title: Quantum Annealing Heuristics for NP-Hard Drug-Target Binding Optimization
abstract: We apply quantum annealing to the drug-target binding optimization problem, formulated as a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO). A neural surrogate model estimates binding energy to guide the annealer; the approach is benchmarked against simulated annealing and genetic algorithm baselines on 200 protein-ligand pairs from the PDBbind dataset.

components.evidence: Information retrieval is not addressed; the paper is entirely within computational chemistry and combinatorial optimization.
A neural surrogate model estimates binding energy from molecular structure encodings, playing a supporting role to the quantum optimizer; no language model is used.
No document-level embeddings are produced; inputs are molecular structure descriptors (SMILES, 3D coordinates), not text.
The optimization output is a ranked list of candidate compounds, which is loosely analogous to recommendation, but the paper does not engage with recommendation system methodology.
Citation network analysis is entirely absent from the paper's scope and evaluation.

title: Adaptive Optimization for Large-Scale Scientific Natural Language Processing
abstract: We propose an adaptive learning rate schedule and gradient accumulation strategy that improves convergence for large-scale scientific NLP pre-training. The method is demonstrated on SciBERT and PubMedBERT training runs and evaluated on six downstream scientific NLP benchmarks including retrieval, classification, and paper recommendation.

components.evidence: The pre-trained models are evaluated on scientific retrieval benchmarks as part of the six-task downstream suite; retrieval is an evaluation target rather than the training objective.
The primary contribution is an improved training recipe for scientific transformer language models; SciBERT and PubMedBERT training dynamics are the subject of study.
Fine-tuned models are used to produce scientific document embeddings evaluated on MTEB-Science; embedding quality is one of the headline downstream metrics.
Paper recommendation is included as one of six downstream evaluation tasks; the recommendation evaluation uses standard collaborative filtering metrics.
Citation-based field-of-study classification is used as one of six downstream benchmarks; citation network structure is not part of the model.

title: Probabilistic Logic and Knowledge Graph Completion for Biomedical Ontologies
abstract: We present a probabilistic logic programming framework that performs knowledge graph completion over biomedical ontologies including MeSH and Gene Ontology. The framework infers missing relations using a combination of logical rules and a neural link predictor (RotatE), with calibrated confidence scores evaluated on standard link prediction benchmarks.

components.evidence: Entities are retrieved from the knowledge graph by logical query resolution rather than by text similarity over a document corpus; this is structured graph lookup, not document retrieval.
RotatE, a neural link predictor, scores candidate triples alongside logical inference; it operates over entity embeddings rather than text, so it is more a graph neural method than a language model.
Entity embeddings in the knowledge graph are trained for link prediction; these are entity-level embeddings rather than document-level representations of scientific papers.
The framework does not address paper or content recommendation; it targets biomedical knowledge graph completion as a distinct task.
Citation network analysis is not used; the paper operates on biomedical knowledge graphs (MeSH, GO) rather than academic citation graphs.
